extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, legal practitioners, researchers, and public commenters on FTC non-compete rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating empirical studies and public comments about the effects of non-competes on innovation, business formation, concentration, prices, and product quality. Emphasizes methodological criteria, outcome measures, and how qualitative comment evidence is weighed alongside empirical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction of principles in Part IV.A.2
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that satisfy the principles described in Part IV.A.2 are given substantial weight by the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission places the greatest weight on studies that meet the methodological principles laid out in Part IV.A.2 (e.g., credible identification, appropriate controls). When a study 'satisfies all the principles described in Part IV.A.2,' it is considered high quality and receives substantial weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible causal identification / control for unrelated factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer studies 'in which factors unrelated to the legal changes at issue are less likely to drive the results.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give more weight to studies that rule out alternate explanations and confounders (e.g., via quasi-experimental designs, difference-in-differences, appropriate controls). Cross-sectional comparisons that could reflect other differences receive less weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of innovation: quantity versus quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that measure only patent quantity receive less weight; measures of patent quality (e.g., citations, value) are a better proxy for innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer outcome measures capturing quality of innovation (patent citations, patent value relative to assets, measures of explorative vs exploitative innovation) rather than raw patent counts alone. Note He study uses patent value as a meaningful proxy and is weighed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional versus quasi-experimental designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely cross-sectional studies are given less weight because results may be due to other differences between places or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-sectional evidence (e.g., comparing California to other states without exploiting legal changes) is less reliable for causal claims; studies using legal changes over time or multiple changes (natural experiments) are more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single legal-change (single-state) designs versus multiple-change designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies relying on a single change in non-compete enforceability (e.g., one state's reform) are given less weight, particularly when accompanied by other contemporaneous legal changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple independent legal changes across jurisdictions increase credibility. Single-state changes that coincide with other policy shifts (e.g., Michigan changes accompanied by other antitrust law changes) make it hard to isolate the effect of non-compete enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of enforceability measurement (continuous vs binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous, granular measures of non-compete enforceability (e.g., Bishara scale) are preferred over binary indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission agrees that more granular measures (the scale based on Bishara (2011)) are stronger; binary measures (enforceable/not enforceable) are less informative and receive less weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal proximity and plausibility of timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Long lags between a legal change and observed effects (e.g., increases occurring ~14 years later) suggest other mechanisms and weaken causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the timing of observed outcomes is plausibly attributable to the legal change; very delayed effects may indicate alternative causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of inference: individual versus aggregate outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that focus on individual behaviors (e.g., inventors taking 'career detours') may inform individual productivity but do not by themselves establish aggregate effects on innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between findings about specific subgroups or behaviors and claims about economy-wide or industry-wide innovation; give greater weight to studies that address aggregate outcomes when assessing overall innovation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether affected parties could anticipate legal changes and adjust behavior prior to the official change, potentially biasing estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural experiments that are 'inadvertent' (less likely anticipated) are more credible; if anticipation is possible, assess direction of bias (may under- or over-estimate true effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and breadth of legal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Small sample sizes and limited variation in legal environments can lead to measurement error; recent studies using broader variation are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer studies that exploit greater breadth of variation (multiple states/changes) and larger samples; take caution with studies whose limited scope may produce noisy estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of co-occurring policy changes (confounding legal changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a change in non-compete enforceability is accompanied by other legal reforms, it is difficult to identify the isolated effect of non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag cases where multiple contemporaneous legal changes occurred (e.g., Michigan reforms accompanied by other antitrust law changes) as lower credibility for isolating non-compete effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional consistency across robust studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission looks for directionally consistent results across the most methodologically robust studies (e.g., multiple studies finding reduced innovation with greater enforceability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in direction across high-quality studies increases confidence in conclusions even if measures and outcomes differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome diversity: beyond patents (new business formation, concentration, prices, quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission assesses a range of outcomes—including new business formation, innovation (quality and quantity), industry concentration, consumer prices, product and service quality, and consumer choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple outcome measures to evaluate net impact; recognize that some outcomes (e.g., product quality, consumer choice) are harder to quantify and may rely more on comment evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence on concentration and prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence linking non-competes to increased concentration and higher consumer prices exists but is less developed than evidence on new business formation and innovation; healthcare is the primary sector with direct price evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission does not rest main findings solely on concentration/price evidence due to limited scope; weigh such studies (e.g., Hausman and Lavetti on physician markets) highly when they meet methodological standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of mechanism plausibility (investment protection vs mobility costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess theoretical mechanisms (e.g., non-competes might incentivize firm investment or might inhibit worker mobility and entrepreneurship) and weigh empirical evidence on net impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether empirical findings align with plausible mechanisms and whether less-restrictive alternatives (trade secrets, NDAs) can protect investments without harming competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of qualitative public comments and anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission gives weight to qualitative evidence from comments when it bolsters empirical findings—e.g., widespread anecdotes from physicians, engineers, and scientists about non-competes stifling innovation or access to care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large volumes of consistent, detailed comment evidence can strengthen conclusions, especially on outcomes that are hard to quantify (product quality, patient access). However, anecdotes without empirical support are weighed in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness of cross-country correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple correlations across countries (e.g., Global Innovation Index vs. non-compete bans) are not persuasive because many other country-level differences can drive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand careful control for confounders and multi-factor explanations; do not rely on raw cross-country comparisons to attribute innovation outcomes to non-compete policy alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of a study to the policy at issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that examine how changes in enforceability map closely to what the final rule does are more probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize evidence that evaluates changes similar in nature to the policy being considered (i.e., reductions in enforceability) rather than distant or only tangentially related institutional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup heterogeneity and generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether effects differ across industries, occupations, or pay levels and whether the most robust studies show negative effects across a range of industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess subgroup results but focus on robust studies' overall patterns; lack of results for every subgroup does not negate general findings if high-quality studies show consistent negative effects across many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of mixed or nuanced findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a study shows mixed results (e.g., increases in exploitative innovation but decreases in explorative innovation), evaluate net impacts and how they relate to growth-oriented innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat mixed internal findings as decisive absent broader corroboration; examine which modes of innovation matter for high-growth outcomes and weigh net effects accordingly.
